title: Sugriva and Vali
hook: the monkey brothers; the arrow through the trees

segments.voice: Yesterday: Shabari, the forest woman who waited years and gave Rama the sweet ones.

Two brothers. The older one, Vali, is king of the monkeys, enormously strong. One night a demon challenges him and runs into a cave, and Vali chases him in, telling his younger brother Sugriva to wait at the entrance. Sugriva waits. Days. Weeks. A whole year. Then blood comes pouring out of the cave, he hears roaring, and he's sure his brother is dead. So he rolls a boulder over the entrance, goes home, and, at the kingdom's urging, becomes king. Then Vali walks out of the cave. Alive. He's won. And the first thing he sees is a rock sealing him in and his little brother on his throne.
screen: `VALI CHASES A DEMON INTO A CAVE.` → `SUGRIVA SEALS IT, THINKING HIM DEAD.` → `VALI WALKS OUT ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Vali doesn't believe it was a mistake. He drives Sugriva out and, in Valmiki's telling, takes Sugriva's wife as well. Sugriva hides on a mountain with a few loyal friends, Hanuman among them. There Rama and Lakshmana find him. Two exiles, each missing a wife, each wronged. They make a pact over a fire: Rama will help Sugriva win back his kingdom, and Sugriva's monkey army will help find Sita. For proof, Rama sends one arrow through a row of seven great sala trees. Sugriva roars a challenge at Vali's gate while Rama waits behind the trees. But the brothers fight, Rama can't tell them apart, and Sugriva is beaten badly. The second time, Sugriva wears a garland of flowers so Rama knows him, and from behind the trees, Rama shoots Vali. Vali falls, furious, with a point. You shot me from hiding, he says. I wasn't even fighting you. Rama answers that Vali took his brother's wife while his brother still lived, and that the land is under Bharata's rule, which Rama is bound to uphold. Vali, dying, accepts it, and asks Rama to look after his son Angada. Remember that name. People have argued about this arrow ever since. Some say Rama upheld dharma, the right order of things, and kept his promise to an ally. Others say it's an act in his story that doesn't sit right. The Ramayana itself lets Vali make his case out loud. The smaller lesson: pick a side in someone else's family fight, and you inherit the whole fight.
screen: `TWO EXILES MAKE A PACT.` · `ONE ARROW THROUGH SEVEN TREES.` · `THE SHOT FROM BEHIND THE TREES.` · `VALI MAKES HIS CASE, OUT LOUD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a fight between two people you love, brothers, sisters, parents, two friends, and don't pick a side yet. Hear each one's story as fairly as you can, and notice where each has a point and where each is hurt. You don't have to fix anything; just hold both stories side by side.
Sugriva, the good-necked one: the younger brother who sealed Vali in a cave by mistake, restored by an arrow people still argue about.
Your line: choose a side carefully. Vali got to make his case, too. Day fifty-five, done.

howItsDone: The killing of Vali is one of the Ramayana episodes Hindu teachers and commentators debate openly; in temple talks, in Ramlila, and in classical commentaries it is taught alongside Vali's objection and Rama's answer.

original.note: Sanskrit: su (good, beautiful) + griva (neck). Sugriva, the one with the handsome neck.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hero shoots a villain.
what it means: two brothers split by a mistake, and a shot from behind the trees that the story lets the dying Vali protest.
what a scholar hears: Vali's objection and Rama's reply are in the Kishkindha Kanda itself; commentators have debated the arrow for centuries.
